The following are reference scripts of past discussions, provided for prior study. 3 transcripts follow. They show how a five-party discussion flows; the participants in them are different people from this session. Learn the discussion flow, pacing, and tone — do not copy lines verbatim.

--- Scripts begin ---

- **Servas**: I worry about our reporting integrity. Who can verify the numbers before we close?
- **Asuka**: The narrative of our past wins feels detached from reality. We need to check retention.
- **Minako**: Cash flow is tight. I need to know what follow-on calls will demand from us.
- **Mio**: We spend too much time sourcing people. I want to see recruiter placement times.
- **Toshio**: Past projects failed due to external delays. I need to understand the delivery risks.
- **Servas**: @Minako, if we borrow against assets, what is the actual collateral value?
- **Asuka**: @Toshio, were the delays technical or logistical? That changes the risk profile.
- **Minako**: @Servas, I am looking at the credit line terms to see what counts as security.
- **Mio**: @Asuka, if retention is low, our exit stories are hollow. I agree with your concern.
- **Toshio**: @Mio, if we can't find staff, the product is irrelevant. I will check delivery records.
- **Servas**: I will look into independent checks on holdings' reported figures to ensure accuracy.
- **Asuka**: I will examine account retention through price rises to see who actually kept customers.
- **Minako**: I will review reserve accounts and follow-on calls to assess our future cash needs.
- **Mio**: I will check retained recruiters' placement times to see who we can actually hire.
- **Toshio**: I will look at delivery records of two holdings to identify the source of delays.

- **Asuka**: Retention data shows our software tools lost a third of accounts during price hikes.
- **Minako**: Our credit line treats subscription contracts as worthless security. We cannot borrow against them.
- **Mio**: Recruiters take four months to place field crews. We cannot staff physical operations quickly.
- **Toshio**: One holding lost five months to a controller shortage. Hardware supply chains are fragile.
- **Servas**: @Minako, if subscriptions are worthless to lenders, our liquidity is trapped in code.
- **Asuka**: @Toshio, the controller shortage confirms that physical hardware is a delivery bottleneck.
- **Minako**: @Servas, this means we need cash reserves, not just equity, for the next two years.
- **Mio**: @Asuka, if we can't keep customers, the exit profile is even worse than I thought.
- **Toshio**: @Mio, the field crew delay means we should avoid companies needing seasonal labor.
- **Servas**: I prefer software that doesn't require physical appraisals. It keeps our quarter-end clean.
- **Asuka**: I am leaning toward the clinic scheduler. It serves independent practices with high retention.
- **Minako**: I am concerned about the harvest sensor. It has hardware, which means appraisal delays.
- **Mio**: The fabric loop needs sorting facilities and crews. That is a nightmare for us.
- **Toshio**: The ledger bridge is pure software. No hardware, no supply chain risks.
- **Servas**: Over
- **Asuka**: Over
- **Minako**: Over
- **Mio**: Over
- **Toshio**: Over
- **Servas**: Candidates are A: Clinic Scheduler, B: Harvest Sensor, C: Fabric Loop, D: Ledger Bridge.
- **Asuka**: A and B have good retention. C and D are risky on different fronts.
- **Minako**: B has hardware. That triggers the appraisal issue I found. I am worried about B.
- **Mio**: C needs field crews. My data says that takes four months. I cannot support C.
- **Toshio**: B has hardware. My data says that causes delivery delays. I am against B.
- **Servas**: D is pure software. No appraisals, no hardware. It fits my reporting needs perfectly.
- **Asuka**: A has high retention. D is software, but I don't have retention data for it yet.
- **Minako**: D is software. No hardware means no appraisal fees. It is safer for our cash flow.
- **Mio**: D is software. No field crews needed. It is the easiest to staff and manage.
- **Toshio**: D is software. No hardware means no supply chain delays. It is the safest delivery.
- **Servas**: I vote for D. It keeps our books clean and avoids the appraisal trap.
- **Asuka**: I vote for A. The retention data is strong, and it is software.
- **Minako**: I vote for D. It avoids the hardware appraisal costs that hurt our liquidity.
- **Mio**: I vote for D. It avoids the staffing nightmare of physical operations.
- **Toshio**: I vote for D. It avoids the delivery risks of hardware supply chains.
- **Servas**: Over
- **Asuka**: Over
- **Minako**: Over
- **Mio**: Over
- **Toshio**: Over

---

- **Toshio**: We need to know which past projects actually worked for the people using them.
- **Victoria**: I am concerned about how long rooms stay out of service during construction.
- **George**: The staff doing the daily upkeep are stretched thin and have had no relief.
- **Mizuki**: Recent projects keep hitting unexpected issues that delay the schedule significantly.
- **Benjamin**: The initial budget figures rarely match the final cost after the building opens.
- **Toshio**: @Victoria, do you have data on how long rooms are unavailable?
- **Victoria**: Yes, I want to check the timetable records for rooms out of service.
- **George**: I should look at the staffing posts since the hiring freeze began.
- **Mizuki**: I will check the weather days in the site diaries to see the delays.
- **Benjamin**: I need to see the tender records over three budget cycles.
- **Toshio**: I will also look at the post-occupancy review ratings to see satisfaction.
- **Victoria**: I will check the booking data for specialist and general rooms.
- **George**: I will also look at the bench technicians' weekly manual routines.
- **Mizuki**: I will also check the decade of delivery schedules by project rationale.
- **Benjamin**: I will also look at the renewal reserve for equipment bought earlier.
- **Toshio**: Over
- **Victoria**: Over
- **George**: Over
- **Mizuki**: Over
- **Benjamin**: Over
- **Toshio**: The post-occupancy reviews show high ratings where any department could book the space.
- **Victoria**: Booking data shows specialist rooms are idle, but general rooms are always full.
- **George**: Technicians spend hours on manual checks because the current equipment is inadequate.
- **Mizuki**: Site diaries show six weeks lost to weather on exposed work last year.
- **Benjamin**: Tender records show mechanical plant costs rising by about a fifth recently.
- **Toshio**: @Victoria, does the booking data support a general-purpose space?
- **Victoria**: Yes, general rooms are turned away all year, while specialist ones sit empty.
- **George**: The staffing freeze means we cannot hire more people to handle new upkeep.
- **Mizuki**: Projects argued for comfort or appeal slip a year or more, unlike inspection fixes.
- **Benjamin**: No renewal reserve was opened for the audiovisual kit bought in the last round.
- **Toshio**: So a space that is widely bookable seems to perform better in reviews.
- **Victoria**: That aligns with the booking data. We need high utilization to justify the cost.
- **George**: But who maintains it? The current staff are already overburdened with manual routines.
- **Mizuki**: If we choose a project with a clear rationale, it might stay on schedule.
- **Benjamin**: We must account for the rising cost of mechanical systems in any new build.
- **Toshio**: Over
- **Victoria**: Over
- **George**: Over
- **Mizuki**: Over
- **Benjamin**: Over
- **Toshio**: Candidate B, the Central Study Commons, fits the high-booking and high-review criteria.
- **Victoria**: I agree. The data shows general rooms are in high demand and underutilized specialist rooms are not.
- **George**: I am worried about the maintenance burden, but the other options seem worse.
- **Mizuki**: A study commons is less exposed to weather than outdoor paths, so it might stay on schedule.
- **Benjamin**: The cost of ventilation for labs is rising, making Candidate A riskier financially.
- **Toshio**: Candidate C, the Path Network, is exposed to weather, which Mizuki noted causes delays.
- **Victoria**: Candidate D, the Media Center, would likely suffer from low booking rates like other specialist rooms.
- **George**: Candidate A requires significant mechanical work, which Benjamin says is getting more expensive.
- **Mizuki**: Candidate B is an indoor conversion, avoiding the weather delays seen in site diaries.
- **Benjamin**: Candidate B avoids the high-cost mechanical plant issues affecting Candidate A.
- **Toshio**: The post-occupancy data strongly favors a space that is widely accessible and bookable.
- **Victoria**: The booking data confirms that general-purpose space is what the campus actually needs.
- **George**: While I have concerns about staffing, Candidate B seems the most logical choice.
- **Mizuki**: The delivery schedule data suggests indoor projects are more reliable than outdoor ones.
- **Benjamin**: From a financial perspective, Candidate B avoids the rising costs of specialized equipment.
- **Toshio**: I am ready to vote.
- **Victoria**: I am ready to vote.
- **George**: I am ready to vote.
- **Mizuki**: I am ready to vote.
- **Benjamin**: I am ready to vote.

---

- **Kenji**: I worry about the ground shifting under the diggers. We need to know what the soil can actually handle.
- **Benjamin**: The park is a living system. I want to see how people actually move through it on a normal day.
- **Minato**: Who is going to mow the grass and fix the fences? I am worried about the daily work.
- **Minako**: Pretty drawings lie. I want to see what the last projects look like after five years of rain.
- **Jonathan**: I am quiet, but I count the coins. I need to know the long-term cost of keeping this place alive.
- **Kenji**: @Benjamin, do you think the paths will hold up if the ground is soft?
- **Benjamin**: @Kenji, only if we respect the drainage. I am checking the crossing patterns to see where the pressure is.
- **Minato**: I am looking at the staff list. It feels like there are fewer people to do the work now.
- **Minako**: I am reviewing the condition of the old works. If the apron cracked, the new one might too.
- **Jonathan**: I am reading the upkeep ledgers. The numbers from three years ago look very different from today.
- **Kenji**: I am checking which firms are still willing to dig here. It seems like a risky job.
- **Benjamin**: I am looking at the heat readings and drainage calls. The ground gets hot and wet, and that matters.
- **Minato**: I am asking about the volunteer groups. Maybe they can help with the small tasks?
- **Minako**: I am looking at the planting records. If the trees died before, we need to know why.
- **Jonathan**: I am checking the terms of the funding. It seems the money has strict rules about what it can buy.
- **Kenji**: Let us see what the ground tells us.
- **Benjamin**: Logic over aesthetics. Let us look at the data.
- **Minato**: I hope we find a plan that is easy to care for.
- **Minako**: Facts will guide us. Let us proceed.
- **Jonathan**: I will keep the ledger open.
- **Kenji**: Only two firms are bidding, and they both warned about clay slippage. The south can be hoarded, but the center cannot.
- **Benjamin**: The counts show people stick to hard ground. The heat readings are high, and drainage calls have doubled. The site is stressed.
- **Minato**: The staff roll is down to seven. But there are two volunteer groups already helping with habitat and youth sports.
- **Minako**: The old basin is fine, but the civic hall apron has been patched three times. Half the avenue trees died from lack of water.
- **Jonathan**: The habitat fund only pays for planting and water, not buildings. And upkeep for planted ground is triple the cost of hard surfaces.
- **Kenji**: @Minako, if the trees died from neglect, does that mean we can't trust the planting plans?
- **Benjamin**: @Kenji, the slippage risk is real. We need a plan that doesn't fight the ground.
- **Minato**: @Jonathan, if upkeep is triple, that is a lot of money. But the volunteers might help with the basic care.
- **Minako**: @Benjamin, the drainage issue is serious. We need something that handles water well, not just looks good.
- **Jonathan**: @Minato, volunteers are great, but they don't pay for specialist water care. The ledger is the truth.
- **Kenji**: The phasing notes say we can keep the park open if we work in stages. That is good for the community.
- **Benjamin**: The heat and drainage data suggest we need more green space to cool the area and absorb rain.
- **Minato**: The volunteer groups are already there. It feels like a natural fit for a plan that uses them.
- **Minako**: The condition of the old works shows that hard surfaces fail. The basin survived because it was designed for water.
- **Jonathan**: The funding terms are strict. We can only build what the fund allows. That limits our options significantly.
- **Kenji**: I am leaning towards a plan that works with the ground, not against it.
- **Benjamin**: The data points to a need for better drainage and cooling.
- **Minato**: I like the idea of using the volunteers. It feels right.
- **Minako**: I am convinced that water management is key.
- **Jonathan**: I am concerned about the long-term cost, but the funding terms are clear.
- **Kenji**: Candidate A, Wetland Restoration, fits the drainage needs and the funding terms. It uses the water, not fights it.
- **Benjamin**: A addresses the heat and drainage issues directly. It is the logical choice based on the data.
- **Minato**: A involves habitat tasks, which the volunteer group already does. It seems like a good match for the people here.
- **Minako**: A is the only plan that aligns with the successful basin design. It is robust and long-lasting.
- **Jonathan**: A is funded by the habitat fund. While upkeep is higher, the capital cost is covered. It is the only viable option financially.
- **Kenji**: @Minako, do you agree that A is the most durable option?
- **Benjamin**: @Kenji, yes. The data supports it. B and D would fail the drainage test.
- **Minato**: @Jonathan, is the upkeep cost really that high? I hope the volunteers can help.
- **Minako**: @Minato, the volunteers help, but the specialist care is bought in. It is a cost, but a necessary one.
- **Jonathan**: @Minato, it is high, but the fund covers the capital. We must accept the ongoing cost for a working system.
- **Kenji**: I am voting for A. It respects the ground and the community.
- **Benjamin**: I am voting for A. It is the only plan that makes sense with the data.
- **Minato**: I am voting for A. It feels like the right choice for the people and the place.
- **Minako**: I am voting for A. It is the most resilient and well-designed option.
- **Jonathan**: I am voting for A. It is the only plan that fits the funding and the long-term reality.
- **Kenji**: Let us move forward with A.
- **Benjamin**: Agreed.
- **Minato**: I am happy with this choice.
- **Minako**: A is the clear winner.
- **Jonathan**: I will monitor the ledger, but A is the right path.

--- Scripts end ---

You are the writer of the discussion described below. You write out the discussion that the participants listed below take part in, under the rules and the flow given.

## Setting
Award of a national grant for basic research in the life sciences. A five-member review panel convened by a national funding agency deliberates over the proposals that reached the final round. One multi-year grant is awarded in this cycle. Participants: Midori, Benjamin, Toshio, Kenji and Servas. Each participant has a concern of their own, which the others do not know.
Things that can be looked into (titles only):
- Travel and bench-fee lines in the ledgers
- National computing agreement and facility day rates
- Incident logs on shared instrumentation
- Station records from partner field sites
- Closeout files of finished awards
- Portfolio review of schedule overruns
- Accreditation and bookings at shared facilities
- National repository deposit turnaround
- Staffing rolls for technical posts
- Minutes on secondments and crew strength

## Discussion format
The talk proceeds in rounds. Each round has 4 turns; in each turn, every participant speaks once, in this fixed order: Servas, Midori, Kenji, Benjamin and Toshio. On a turn, a participant either speaks, says "Skip" (passes this turn only), or says "Over" (takes no further turns this round). A participant can address another directly with @Name, to ask them a question, answer theirs, agree with them, or object to what they said. An utterance is anywhere from 1 to 40 words; give it the length and content that suit the moment. An utterance consists only of the participant's own words: no name labels, headings, stage directions or commentary, and no speaking for others. The talk is a conversation among the participants: they respond to one another, asking, answering, agreeing and objecting, and the decision grows out of that exchange.

## Schedule
| Round | Start of the round | Talk | End of the round |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | nothing new (the things that can be looked into are listed above, titles only) | 4 turns | each participant chooses 2 of the listed things to look into |
| 2 | each participant is told what they found out (that participant only) | 4 turns | nothing |
| 3 | everyone is told the candidates | 4 turns | every participant votes; the candidate with the most votes is selected |
- Several participants may choose the same thing; what is found out is told only to the participant who looked into it.
If votes are tied, one of the tied candidates is chosen by a fixed rule. The discussion ends after the vote.

## Looking into things
After round 1, each participant chooses 2 of the listed things to look into. What they find out is told only to that participant.

## Participants
Name: Midori
Age: 38
Gender: female
Personality: Midori has a calm and kind personality. She is friendly to everyone and listens to the concerns and problems of those around her, offering reliable advice. She can be a little shy, often acting reserved with people she meets for the first time, but once she opens up, she shows her bright and energetic side. She loves cooking and has a domestic side, but she also has a spirit of adventure and enjoys trying new things. She values balance in both her work and personal life and places importance on harmony with those around her.
Concern: Every cycle the headline award looks the same size, yet what it actually buys keeps shrinking in some places and holding steady in others. Before ranking anything, I want to know which kinds of spending the agency still absorbs centrally and which now land on the awardee.

Name: Benjamin
Age: 28
Gender: male
Personality: Benjamin is an intelligent and calm person. He is able to think calmly and rationally, and even in emotional situations, he places importance on logic. In public, he is elegant and polite, often incorporating sarcasm and humor into his conversations, but he is skilled at doing so without hurting others, creating a harmonious atmosphere. He also has an introverted side, often engrossed in deep thought, and occasionally keeps his distance from those around him. However, his calmness and knowledge are factors that earn him the trust of others even in difficult situations.
Concern: Too many recent awards lost time to things that had nothing to do with the science itself, and the panel usually hears about it only after the money is committed. It seemed worth asking in advance where work in this field actually gets interrupted.

Name: Toshio
Age: 28
Gender: male
Personality: Toshio has a calm and calculating personality and does not often show his emotions. He has a strong will and is the type of person who steadily moves toward his goals. He tends to take a step back from those around him, is not very assertive, and has an air of mystery about him. Occasionally, he observes things with a sharp gaze and has the ability to quickly assess situations. As a result, he is trusted by others as a reliable presence, but he is cautious about getting deeply involved with others. It seems that he has experienced some pain or suffering in his past, but he rarely shows it to others, and those scars may be connected to his cold-hearted side.
Concern: Our judgements about promise have not aged well, and some of us have watched confident picks quietly stall while plainer ones kept earning their keep. Rather than trust that instinct once more, I went back through what finished awards here actually delivered and when.

Name: Kenji
Age: 12
Gender: male
Personality: Kenji is curious and actively takes on challenges. He values his friends and enjoys communicating with those around him. Although he can be a little clumsy at times, he is always positive and never abandons those in need. He is easygoing and well-liked by those around him.
Concern: Nothing funded here runs in isolation, since it lands on shared facilities and services that no single award pays to expand. Given how often that spare capacity has been the thing that gives way, I looked at what state those services are in right now.

Name: Servas
Age: 85
Gender: male
Personality: Servas has a very calm and composed personality. Based on the knowledge and experience he has gained over the years, he often gives advice to those around him. He is an excellent listener and can talk openly with anyone. He also occasionally expresses deep philosophical thoughts, and his words inspire many people. He is full of vitality and always gives positive energy to those around him.
Concern: Money can be voted through in an afternoon, while the trained hands a project needs take years to gather and can disappear in a season. That worry sent me to the question of who is genuinely available around here now, and who has already gone.

## Hidden information
The candidates and the full text of every card are listed here. The participants do not know them before the schedule above says so, and nothing from them may appear in the talk before the round in which it is revealed.

Candidates (see the schedule above):
- A: Microbiome Atlas. A project cataloging microbial communities in soil samples collected across several climate zones and publishing the resulting sequences together with standardized site metadata.
- B: Plant Drought Signaling. Research into the molecular signals that crops use to detect water shortage, conducted through controlled greenhouse trials across several cultivars and soil conditions.
- C: Protein Folding Dynamics. A study of how selected membrane proteins change shape over time, combining laboratory spectroscopy with simulation in order to describe intermediate structural states.
- D: Regeneration in Amphibians. An investigation of limb regrowth in salamander species, tracking cell populations and signaling activity through the successive stages of tissue restoration.

Cards (see the schedule above; title: text):
- Travel and bench-fee lines in the ledgers: Ledgers show the vehicle-hire and per-diem lines frozen for three seasons while shipping charges climbed, though the ministry extended its bench-fee subsidy for glasshouse space.
- National computing agreement and facility day rates: The renewed national computing agreement covers simulation and modelling hours at no charge, while animal-unit day rates rose sharply after last year's vivarium rebuild.
- Incident logs on shared instrumentation: Incident logs record the shared spectroscopy suite standing idle eleven weeks last year after its service contract lapsed; one engineer now covers three institutes.
- Station records from partner field sites: Station records show three of the five partner field sites losing a whole season to flooding or fire, while indoor holding rooms ran through uninterrupted.
- Closeout files of finished awards: Closeout files show catalogue-style awards here still drawing outside users a decade on, while several mechanism-focused ones ended with their central question unresolved.
- Portfolio review of schedule overruns: A portfolio review found awards built on live breeding colonies overran schedule twice as often as those whose main risk sat in computation rather than biology.
- Accreditation and bookings at shared facilities: The animal facility cleared its accreditation renewal in spring and gained resident veterinary cover, while glasshouse blocks are booked solid through two more growing cycles.
- National repository deposit turnaround: The national repository finished its long migration, so deposits that once waited most of a year now clear review inside a few weeks.
- Staffing rolls for technical posts: Staffing rolls show most trained phenotyping technicians left for industry over two years, while applicants for modelling and code posts now arrive in numbers.
- Minutes on secondments and crew strength: Minutes note both senior modelling analysts are seconded abroad until next autumn, while the glasshouse crew came through the restructuring at full strength.

Write the complete transcript of the discussion in the exact Markdown format specified. Output only the transcript.

## Output format
Markdown, exactly this structure; nothing before or after it:

(one line per participant, in the fixed speaking order; repeat for Turn 2, 3 and 4; a participant who said Over has no line in the later turns of that round)
### Action
- investigate: <Name> -> <card title>; <card title>
(one line per participant; titles exactly as listed)
## Round 2
### Talk
(4 turns as above)
## Round 3
### Talk
(4 turns as above)
### Vote
- <voter name> -> <candidate label>
(one line per participant)
